title: TRI-611 and the Serendipity of Molecular-Glue Discovery
TRI-611 and the Serendipity of Molecular-Glue Discovery
text:
The central result
ALK-positive cancers have benefited enormously from tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), especially lorlatinib. But resistance mutations accumulate around the kinase active site, CNS disease remains important, and inhibitors that compete for the same orthosteric pocket cannot easily be combined.
The study by Conery and colleagues presents an orthogonal strategy: instead of inhibiting ALK, eliminate it. The authors identify TRI-611, a selective, brain-penetrant molecular glue degrader that recruits ALK to the CRL4–CRBN E3 ligase.

title: TRI-611 and the Serendipity of Molecular-Glue Discovery
text:
A model molecular-glue workflow
The authors screened 4,827 compounds designed to bind CRBN using TR-FRET to detect compounds that induce proximity between CRBN and the ALK kinase domain. The initial hit, Compound 1, induced proximity but did not yet degrade ALK. Medicinal-chemistry optimization ultimately produced TRI-611.
The final molecule was validated through multiple complementary approaches: TR-FRET, surface plasmon resonance, cellular NanoBiT assays, ubiquitination studies, proteomics, CRBN knockout, structural biology, cellular pharmacology, and in vivo PK/PD and efficacy studies.
This progression is important. A molecular glue is not simply a compound that binds two proteins. It must create a productive ternary complex with the right geometry, cooperativity, and ubiquitination orientation.
TRI-611 induced rapid and deep degradation of ALK fusion proteins. ALK levels fell by approximately 90% within one to two hours, and degradation required CRBN, neddylation, and the proteasome. Proteomic profiling showed strong selectivity across the tested cell lines, including no significant degradation of related kinases such as ROS1 or the NTRK family.

title: TRI-611 and the Serendipity of Molecular-Glue Discovery
section: A new degron outside the kinase active site
text:
A new degron outside the kinase active site
The structural centerpiece is a 2.7 Å cryo-EM structure of the ALK–TRI-611–CRBN complex.



Figure 2a. Cryo-EM structure of the ALK–TRI-611–CRBN ternary complex.





Figure 2b. TRI-611 interaction footprint compared with ALK inhibitor binding sites and resistance mutations.





Figure 2c. Molecular interactions at the ALK–TRI-611–CRBN interface.


Figure 2 from Conery et al. The three panels are shown separately for readability: the ternary complex, the spatial relationship between the glue interface and TKI resistance mutations, and the key molecular contacts. Reproduced from the supplied paper for commentary and analysis; structural coordinates are deposited as PDB 9XZG.
Unlike a PROTAC, TRI-611 does not use a long flexible linker to connect two independently binding ligands. Instead, it creates a chemically shaped surface that is complementary to both proteins.
TRI-611 engages the C-lobe of the ALK kinase domain, far from the ATP-binding site. Key interactions include contacts involving ALK Tyr1385, Arg1382, and Asp1389. The authors describe this recognition element as a previously undescribed “turn–helix degron,” distinct from the better-known CRBN G-loop and G-loop-like degrons.
This expands the structural landscape of CRBN recognition. It suggests that molecular-glue discovery need not be limited to proteins containing obvious canonical degrons.

title: TRI-611 and the Serendipity of Molecular-Glue Discovery
section: Why TRI-611 can overcome ALK TKI resistance
text:
Why TRI-611 can overcome ALK TKI resistance
Most clinically important ALK resistance mutations affect the kinase active site or its surroundings. Because TRI-611 engages a separate surface, mutations such as L1196M, G1202R, I1171N, and compound resistance mutations do not necessarily prevent degradation.
The authors tested TRI-611 in engineered Ba/F3 models, endogenous CRISPR-edited NCI-H3122 cells, and patient-derived cell lines. TRI-611 retained activity across a broad panel of ALK variants and was particularly more potent than lorlatinib in models derived from patients who had progressed on lorlatinib.
The in vivo results were similarly strong. TRI-611 induced regression in subcutaneous xenografts containing resistant ALK variants, including L1196M/G1202R. It also produced dose-dependent responses in intracranial models, including tumors carrying the same lorlatinib-resistant mutation.
This is one of the strongest aspects of the study: the structural hypothesis is connected directly to resistant cellular models, patient-derived models, tumor pharmacodynamics, and CNS efficacy.

title: TRI-611 and the Serendipity of Molecular-Glue Discovery
text:
Combining degradation with inhibition
Because TRI-611/CRBN and ALK TKIs engage different regions of the kinase domain, the two mechanisms should be compatible. The authors report that TRI-611–CRBN engagement does not alter ALK enzyme kinetics and that ALK TKIs retain activity when ALK is in the TRI-611–CRBN complex.
The combination therefore raises an interesting mechanistic question. Does TRI-611/CRBN binding have any effect on ALK kinase activity under conditions in which neddylation is blocked by MLN4924? Such an experiment could separate formation of the ternary complex from activation of the CRL4–CRBN degradation machinery. It would also clarify whether the glue-bound complex itself changes ALK conformation or catalytic behavior.
Similarly, does TRI-611/CRBN binding alter the biochemical potency or residence time of lorlatinib? The available data suggest that it does not prevent orthosteric inhibition, but a more detailed biochemical analysis would establish whether the two ligands are entirely independent or subtly influence one another.
In cells, TRI-611 shifted the lorlatinib dose-response curve and produced greater-than-additive growth inhibition at partially active concentrations. In mouse models, subefficacious doses of the two agents produced tumor regression, and combination treatment delayed tumor regrowth after dosing stopped.
The latter result is consistent with deeper or more durable tumor control, although delayed regrowth alone does not prove that more tumor cells were permanently eliminated.

title: TRI-611 and the Serendipity of Molecular-Glue Discovery
text:
Molecular-glue discovery remains highly serendipitous
The authors identified a productive CRBN-based glue by screening 4,827 CRBN-binding compounds for ALK–CRBN proximity, even though ALK did not contain an obvious canonical G-loop degron. The probability of finding such a molecule cannot be calculated from this study alone, but the success rate for discovering a functional glue against a specific target is generally expected to be low.
There is also a fundamental limitation to the screening format. TR-FRET requires purified protein, yet full-length purified proteins are often difficult or impossible to obtain. Researchers may therefore need to screen individual domains or engineered constructs.
If the relevant degron is absent from the purified domain, depends on a fusion partner, is exposed only in a particular conformational state, or requires a native protein environment, a genuine molecular glue may not produce a screening signal. A negative screen may therefore reflect limitations of the protein construct rather than the true inability of the target to form a productive degrader complex.
TRI-611 is an excellent success story, but it does not make this discovery process predictable. It shows that unusual degrons can be found; it does not tell us where the next one will come from.

title: TRI-611 and the Serendipity of Molecular-Glue Discovery
text:
What remains unresolved
The selectivity data are impressive, but they do not completely exclude lineage-specific degradation in other human tissues. This is particularly important for SALL4, a CRBN neosubstrate associated with teratogenic biology.
SALL4 is probably absent or expressed at very low levels in the cell lines used for the proteomic experiments. Consequently, the absence of SALL4 degradation in those datasets cannot be interpreted as evidence that TRI-611 will not degrade SALL4 in human tissues where SALL4 is expressed.
For a CRBN molecular glue, this is a major development question. A stronger safety package should include quantitative proteomics in additional differentiated and primary human cell types, SALL4-specific degradation assays, developmental and reproductive toxicity models, and broader evaluation in tissues with relevant CRBN-neosubstrate expression.
TRI-611 may also avoid classical TKI-resistance mutations while creating a resistance surface of its own. Mutations that disrupt the ALK–TRI-611–CRBN interface could theoretically preserve ALK kinase function while preventing degradation. Chronic resistance-selection studies will be important.

title: TRI-611 and the Serendipity of Molecular-Glue Discovery
text:
Final perspective
The most important contribution of this study is not simply that TRI-611 shrinks ALK-positive tumors. Several ALK inhibitors can do that.
The deeper contribution is that an oncogenic kinase fusion can be eliminated by a brain-penetrant molecular glue through a non-orthosteric structural degron. That mechanism bypasses many classical active-site resistance mutations and permits simultaneous kinase inhibition and protein degradation.
TRI-611 is therefore both a promising therapeutic concept and a model discovery story. It shows what a complete molecular-glue program can achieve, while also showing how much of the initial discovery process still depends on finding the right protein construct, conformational state, E3 ligase, and chemical geometry.

title: Why the source of protein overexpression matters for degraders
Why the source of protein overexpression matters for degraders
text:
What this paper adds
Gudauskaitė and colleagues studied how two routes to high β-catenin expression affect induced degradation. Cancer-associated mutations that stabilize β-catenin raised its baseline abundance, yet dTAG treatment drove the mutant and wild-type proteins toward similar residual levels. Increasing transcription produced a different result: protein abundance remained higher both before and after treatment. 1
My initial reaction was that the main conclusion is not especially new. Protein-turnover models already predict that changing synthesis and changing intrinsic degradation will have different effects under degrader treatment. The authors recognize this connection and cite earlier modeling work, including Bartlett and Gilbert’s 2022 review. 2
The paper still adds useful evidence. It tests both routes to overexpression in a controlled cellular system and shows why percentage degradation can be misleading. For drug development, the amount of functional protein left after treatment may matter more than the percentage removed.

title: Why the source of protein overexpression matters for degraders
section: Two routes to high β-catenin expression
text:
Two routes to high β-catenin expression
The authors fused β-catenin to FKBP12 F36V and GFP. The dTAG compounds recruit an E3 ligase to the FKBP12 tag, while GFP provides a readout of target abundance. Each construct was integrated at the same genomic landing site in engineered 293 cells, reducing differences in expression context that would complicate a comparison across unrelated cell lines. 1
Three cancer-associated mutations, S45F, T41A, and S33F, raised baseline reporter abundance by approximately threefold, fourfold, and fivefold. These mutations impair the native degradation pathway. After recruitment of either VHL or CRBN, the large pretreatment differences narrowed, and the proteins approached similar residual levels during prolonged treatment, including the 24-hour measurements at 100 nM.
The authors then used a doxycycline-inducible system to increase production. Doxycycline raised pretreatment protein expression approximately 2.4-fold for wild-type β-catenin and 4.9-fold for S45F. After 24 hours of dTAGv1 treatment at 100 nM, Figure 4G shows approximately 3.3-fold and 4.7-fold higher residual signals in the induced cells. The fractional depletion was similar with and without induction. 1
The paper calls these “absolute” protein levels, but the measurement is background-corrected GFP fluorescence rather than calibrated molecules per cell. The comparison is valid within the reporter system. It does not establish how much β-catenin would remain in a tumor or whether that amount would sustain signaling.

title: Why the source of protein overexpression matters for degraders
text:
The model predicts the result
Bartlett and Gilbert’s 2022 review discussed quantitative PK-PD frameworks for protein degraders. Haid and Reichel’s 2023 framework made the relationship among target engagement, endogenous turnover, and induced degradation explicit. Their Equation 8 uses the indirect-response formulation also discussed by Bartlett and Gilbert. 2, 3
Using the notation from my earlier degradability analysis, the protein balance is:
\[
\frac{dP}{dt}=k_{sp}-k_{dp}P-k_{cat}[PLE].
\]
Here, \(k_{sp}\) is the synthesis rate, \(k_{dp}\) is the endogenous first-order loss constant, and \(k_{cat}[PLE]\) is the induced degradation flux through the target-degrader-E3 complex.
For intuition, assume that synthesis and exposure are constant and that the E3 ligase is not saturated. If ternary engagement, \(TE=[PLE]/P\), is approximately constant, then \(k_{ind}=k_{cat}TE\) and:
\[
P_0=\frac{k_{sp}}{k_{dp}},
\qquad
P_{ss,drug}=\frac{k_{sp}}{k_{dp}+k_{ind}}.
\]
These equations are a simplified interpretation, not a fit to the paper’s data. They are useful because they separate two ways of reaching the same high baseline.
A stabilizing mutation lowers \(k_{dp}\). If synthesis is unchanged, the baseline rises. When induced degradation is much faster than endogenous turnover, the treated level approaches \(k_{sp}/k_{ind}\) and becomes relatively insensitive to the original half-life. This explains why the stabilized mutants can approach the wild-type residual level.
The convergence is approximate. With the same finite \(k_{ind}\), the model still predicts somewhat more residual protein when \(k_{dp}\) is lower. The result fits a kinetic regime in which induced degradation dominates endogenous turnover. It does not show that stabilization can never affect the residual level.
Increasing synthesis changes the numerator instead. If synthesis rises fivefold while both loss constants remain unchanged, the model predicts fivefold more protein before and after treatment. This is the pattern seen in the inducible system. It does not require saturation of the E3 ligase or proteasome.

title: Why the source of protein overexpression matters for degraders
text:
Why Dmax can mislead
Under the same assumptions, fractional steady-state depletion at a specified exposure is:
\[
D_{ss}=1-\frac{P_{ss,drug}}{P_0}
=\frac{k_{ind}}{k_{dp}+k_{ind}}.
\]
The synthesis term cancels. More synthesis raises the amount of protein remaining without necessarily changing the fraction removed. \(D_{max}\) is the greatest depletion observed across the tested conditions, so a finite-time experimental \(D_{max}\) should not automatically be treated as the steady-state value in this equation.
Consider a simple calculation with synthesis of 100 arbitrary protein units per hour, endogenous loss of 1 per hour, and induced loss of 4 per hour:

These are calculated examples, not experimental measurements. The two overexpressing conditions begin with the same amount of protein but finish at very different levels. The stabilization condition also produces a larger percentage reduction because its endogenous loss rate is lower.
An 80% \(D_{max}\) does not identify a unique post-treatment protein level. A 95% \(D_{max}\) in one cell and 80% in another also does not prove that the first cell has a more efficient ubiquitin-proteasome system. Different endogenous turnover rates can change the percentage even when the induced degradation rate is the same.
The residual levels will not always converge. If the induced loss constant in the example were only 1 per hour, fivefold stabilization would leave about 83 units rather than 50 units in the reference condition. The common floor reported in this paper depends on induced degradation being strong relative to endogenous turnover.
Haid and Reichel similarly found that baseline target abundance has little effect on fractional degradation in their unsaturated approximation. That conclusion does not make abundance irrelevant. Baseline abundance can cancel from a normalized response while still determining how much protein remains. 3

title: Why the source of protein overexpression matters for degraders
section: What the study does not show
text:
What the study does not show
Equations cannot tell us whether their assumptions will hold in a cell, where a mutation may change localization or accessibility and high expression may strain the degradation machinery. This is where the paper earns some credit. Similar results with VHL-recruiting and CRBN-recruiting dTAG compounds make the experimental finding more convincing.
Still, both compounds recruit ligases through an engineered FKBP12 tag. The study does not test whether a therapeutic degrader binding native β-catenin would maintain the same target engagement and productive ubiquitination across these variants.
The experiment also does not demonstrate degrader resistance. Increased synthesis left more reporter protein after treatment, but the authors did not show that the residual pool maintained Wnt signaling, cell growth, or tumor survival. Doxycycline induction models increased expression; it is not evidence that gene amplification arose under degrader selection.
I see this paper as a validation study rather than a new mechanistic framework. It gives experimental support to a point already present in the modeling literature: high baseline abundance has to be separated into synthesis and turnover, and \(D_{max}\) should be interpreted together with the amount of target remaining. Until residual protein is linked to persistent pathway activity, the proposed connection to drug resistance remains a hypothesis.

Evidence note
The experimental systems, fold changes, treatment conditions, and reporter outcomes come from Gudauskaitė and colleagues. I derived the equations and illustrative table under assumptions of constant synthesis, first-order loss, steady state, and unsaturated, constant engagement. The assessment of conceptual novelty and the interpretation of the resistance claim are my own.

title: How photoproximity labeling uncovered a hidden regulator of c-Myc
text:
iLo

2026-09-04
c-Myc is one of the best-studied cancer proteins, yet it remains difficult to drug directly. One alternative is to identify proteins that cancer cells use to maintain c-Myc expression or stability. The study by Milione and colleagues takes this approach and finds SLK—a kinase that conventional mutation- or expression-centered searches would have been unlikely to prioritize [1].
What interested me most was not simply the addition of another kinase to the c-Myc network. It was why SLK had escaped detection for so long.

title: How photoproximity labeling uncovered a hidden regulator of c-Myc
section: The relevant signal was invisible to conventional databases
text:
The relevant signal was invisible to conventional databases
SLK would not stand out as an obvious cancer driver in a typical bioinformatics analysis. It is not commonly defined by recurrent cancer mutations, strong gene amplification, or a striking increase in bulk RNA or protein abundance. Although SLK and c-Myc show some degree of co-dependency in certain cancer cell lines, co-dependency alone does not reveal the biological connection between them.
The paper suggests that the important variable is neither total SLK expression nor mutation status. It is which SLK isoform is expressed and where that isoform is located.
PC-3 cells preferentially express SLK-L, a longer splice isoform containing exon 13 and a putative nuclear localization signal. Total SLK abundance was similar among the prostate cell lines examined, but nuclear SLK was elevated in PC-3 cells. This brings SLK into the same compartment as c-Myc and creates an opportunity for a functional interaction [1].
This is the type of relationship that conventional cancer databases are poorly equipped to uncover. Gene-level RNA analysis often combines multiple transcripts into one value. Standard proteomics may quantify total SLK without reliably distinguishing SLK-L from SLK-S. Even a dependency screen can tell us only that a cell needs SLK. It cannot explain whether that dependency involves c-Myc, mitosis, focal adhesions, or another SLK function.

My interpretation. The paper supports SLK-L as the likely c-Myc-relevant isoform. It does not establish that only SLK-L can stabilize c-Myc, because the authors did not directly compare the two isoforms in a controlled rescue experiment. SLK-S might also support c-Myc if it were artificially directed into the nucleus. That distinction would show whether exon 13 contributes a unique molecular function or mainly provides nuclear access.

The broader conclusion is persuasive: a cancer dependency can arise from altered splicing and localization without producing a conspicuous change in total RNA or protein. A database search centered on mutation and expression would probably never have prioritized SLK as a c-Myc regulator.

title: How photoproximity labeling uncovered a hidden regulator of c-Myc
section: A short snapshot of the c-Myc neighborhood
text:
A short snapshot of the c-Myc neighborhood
The authors found SLK using µMap, a photoproximity-labeling method. They attached an iridium photocatalyst to c-Myc in biochemically intact isolated nuclei, added a diazirine-biotin probe, and irradiated the sample with blue light for one minute. Light activation generated short-lived reactive carbenes that labeled proteins close to c-Myc—within an estimated radius of approximately 4 nm in this implementation [1,2].
This short labeling period is important. Methods such as BioID use a promiscuous biotin ligase and typically integrate proximity over much longer labeling windows [3]. That broad history can be useful, but it also creates a larger candidate list when the bait is a mobile nuclear protein associated with extensive chromatin complexes.
In a same-cell-line comparison in PC-3 cells, BioID yielded 1,563 proteins and µMap yielded 519. Both methods recovered comparable numbers of known c-Myc interactions, but SLK was enriched by µMap and not identified by BioID [1]. The smaller µMap result reduced the candidate space by roughly threefold.
The comparison does not prove that spatial resolution alone explains the difference. The experiments also differed in labeling duration, cellular compartment, fusion design, reaction chemistry, acquisition method, and proteasome-inhibitor treatment. BioID was performed in whole cells over 24 hours, whereas µMap captured a one-minute interval in isolated nuclei [1].
For me, the value of µMap is therefore not simply that it labels a smaller radius. Its more useful feature is experimental control. The investigator can choose the compartment and the moment in which the protein neighborhood is recorded. This may help uncover low-abundance or conditional interactions that disappear inside a large, time-integrated interactome.

title: How photoproximity labeling uncovered a hidden regulator of c-Myc
section: How strongly does SLK regulate c-Myc?
text:
How strongly does SLK regulate c-Myc?
The functional data go well beyond the initial proximity signal. SLK co-immunoprecipitated with c-Myc in PC-3 cells. Knocking out SLK reduced c-Myc protein to approximately 20% of the wild-type level, while the reduction in MYC RNA was much smaller [1].
The c-Myc half-life decreased from 138 minutes to 60 minutes after SLK knockout. Under a first-order degradation model, the degradation-rate ratio is:
\[
\frac{k_{\mathrm{KO}}}{k_{\mathrm{WT}}}
= \frac{\ln 2 / 60}{\ln 2 / 138}
= \frac{138}{60}
\approx 2.3
\]
This derived estimate corresponds to an approximately 2.3-fold increase in the apparent degradation rate. Re-expressing c-Myc rescued target-gene expression, proliferation, cell-cycle progression, and cellular morphology after SLK loss. SLK-knockout cells also failed to establish tumors in the reported PC-3 xenograft experiment [1].
Together, these experiments make a strong case that SLK supports c-Myc stability and c-Myc-dependent growth in PC-3 cells.

title: How photoproximity labeling uncovered a hidden regulator of c-Myc
section: The proposed mechanism is not yet closed
text:
The proposed mechanism is not yet closed
The authors propose that SLK phosphorylates c-Myc at serine 329, which reduces GSK3β-dependent phosphorylation at threonine 58 and protects c-Myc from degradation. Recombinant SLK phosphorylated c-Myc at S329 in vitro; an S329A c-Myc mutant was less stable, whereas the phosphomimetic S329D mutant was more stable. In vitro experiments and a cellular proximity-ligation assay also support competition between SLK and GSK3β for c-Myc binding [1].
However, the paper does not demonstrate that endogenous S329 phosphorylation falls after SLK knockout. It also does not show that wild-type SLK rescues c-Myc stability while kinase-dead SLK fails to do so. SLK may phosphorylate c-Myc directly in cells, but it could also stabilize c-Myc partly by acting as a scaffold or by interfering with GSK3β binding.

The experiment I would run next
Compare SLK-L, kinase-dead SLK-L, SLK-S, and nuclear-targeted SLK-S in SLK-knockout PC-3 cells. Measure endogenous c-Myc S329 and T58 phosphorylation together with c-Myc half-life.

If only catalytically active SLK-L rescues the phenotype, kinase activity and isoform context are both required.
If nuclear-targeted SLK-S rescues, exon 13 may act mainly through localization.
If kinase-dead nuclear SLK still provides partial rescue, scaffolding or competition with GSK3β probably contributes.


That comparison would separate catalytic activity from localization and scaffolding.

title: How photoproximity labeling uncovered a hidden regulator of c-Myc
section: Could µMap help identify E3-ligase substrates?
text:
Could µMap help identify E3-ligase substrates?
The study also made me think about a broader application. Photoproximity labeling may be particularly useful for finding substrates of E3 ubiquitin ligases.
E3–substrate interactions are often weak and transient. Once ubiquitinated, the substrate may leave the ligase complex and be degraded rapidly. A long labeling window can accumulate many proteins that share a compartment with the E3 ligase but are not substrates. A short pulse could provide a cleaner snapshot of proteins present near the ligase during substrate recognition.
Compartment control would add another advantage. The same E3 ligase can encounter different substrates in the nucleus, cytoplasm, or at specific membranes. Restricting µMap to one compartment could reduce unrelated proteins and expose context-specific substrates.

Proposed application—not established by this paper. Proximity alone would not show that a labeled protein is an E3 substrate. Useful controls would include a ligase-dead mutant, acute proteasome inhibition, time-resolved labeling, and direct measurements of ubiquitination or protein stability. Comparing active and inactive ligases could distinguish proteins that merely occupy the same space from proteins whose proximity depends on catalytic substrate engagement.

That may be where photoproximity labeling has its greatest value. It does not replace genetics, biochemistry, or ubiquitin proteomics. It gives those methods a shorter and more biologically focused list of candidates to test.

title: How photoproximity labeling uncovered a hidden regulator of c-Myc
text:
What would change my mind?
My interpretation would weaken if controlled isoform-rescue experiments showed that SLK-S supports c-Myc stability without nuclear localization, if loss of SLK left endogenous c-Myc S329 phosphorylation unchanged under conditions with verified assay sensitivity, or if the SLK–c-Myc dependency failed to reproduce beyond the reported cellular contexts.
The current study nevertheless illustrates a useful principle. SLK was not hidden because nobody had measured its RNA or protein. It was hidden because the relevant biology depended on an isoform entering the right compartment and approaching c-Myc during a limited interaction window. µMap provided a way to see that event.

Evidence note
Reported: interactome sizes, localization, co-immunoprecipitation, knockout effects, half-lives, rescue experiments, xenograft outcome, and the biochemical S329/GSK3β experiments come from Milione and colleagues [1].
Derived: the approximately 2.3-fold change in apparent degradation rate is calculated above from the reported half-lives, assuming first-order degradation.
Inferred: SLK-L is probably the c-Myc-relevant isoform, but isoform specificity and the necessity of SLK catalytic activity remain incompletely tested.
Proposed: the E3-ligase application and the four-arm SLK rescue experiment are the author’s suggestions.

title: About iLo
text:
Cartoon portrait of I-Chung Lo, who writes as iLo





Translational scientist · Writer of The Edge of Evidence
I-Chung Lo, writing as iLo, is a translational scientist interested in how biological evidence becomes decisions in drug discovery and development. The Edge of Evidence examines what scientific findings support, what they leave unresolved, and what they may mean for new medicines.
The publication is written for biotech and pharma scientists and scientifically literate industry professionals. Its purpose is not to summarize every result. It is to identify the decision-relevant evidence, expose the assumptions connecting experiments to claims, and ask what measurement would resolve the remaining uncertainty.

I-Chung Lo, writing as iLo, is a translational scientist interested in how biological evidence becomes decisions in drug discovery and development. The Edge of Evidence examines what scientific findings support, what they leave unresolved, and what they may mean for new medicines.
The publication is written for biotech and pharma scientists and scientifically literate industry professionals. Its purpose is not to summarize every result. It is to identify the decision-relevant evidence, expose the assumptions connecting experiments to claims, and ask what measurement would resolve the remaining uncertainty.

title: What a degradability landscape can tell us about protein degraders
What a degradability landscape can tell us about protein degraders
text:
The central assessment
Du and colleagues present a framework for organizing the factors that determine protein degradation. Its effective processing constant, kpr, serves much the same mathematical role as the catalytic constant in earlier models. The framework is useful, but the paper does not establish that kpr is a superior predictive or mechanistic parameter.
Targeted protein degradation creates an appealing optimization problem. A compound must bring a target and an E3 ligase together, enable productive ubiquitination, and remove protein faster than the cell replaces it. Binding affinity measures only part of that process. DMAX and DC50 summarize its outcome, but do not directly identify the limiting step.
In A quantitative approach for defining the degradability landscape of protein degraders, Du and colleagues connect these processes in a compact model 1. They calculate ternary-complex abundance, combine it with endogenous protein turnover, and introduce an effective processing constant, Kpr. Varying target affinity and this constant produces a landscape of predicted degradation depth and potency.
What interested me most was whether this framework adds explanatory power beyond the mathematics already available, and whether its validation supports using fitted parameters to guide chemistry.
The paper deserves credit for making a complicated system easier to explore. My concern is the biological meaning assigned to a parameter estimated from the very degradation response it is intended to explain.

title: What a degradability landscape can tell us about protein degraders
section: How much is new in the rate constant?
text:
How much is new in the rate constant?
The authors describe target abundance using a balance between synthesis, natural turnover, and degrader-induced loss:
\[
\frac{dP}{dt}=k_{\mathrm{sp}}-k_{\mathrm{dp}}P-k_{\mathrm{pr}}[PLE].
\]
Here, [PLE] is the modeled target-degrader-E3 complex. The product kpr[PLE] is the induced degradation flux. The constant represents processing per unit of ternary complex, rather than disappearance of the entire target pool.
That distinction is valid. More target can generate more ternary complex and a larger absolute degradation flux without requiring the processing constant to change. The underlying turnover logic, however, is not new; it has been represented in several earlier mathematical and pharmacodynamic models.
Haid and Reichel’s 2023 framework already expressed the same balance using a catalytic constant and ternary target engagement 2. Defining \(p=P/P_0\) and \(TE=[PLE]/P\), Du’s equation becomes:
\[
\frac{dp}{dt}=k_{\mathrm{dp}}(1-p)-k_{\mathrm{pr}}TE\,p.
\]
This is the earlier turnover equation with kpr occupying the role of kcat. Haid and Reichel’s framework also includes binding affinities, cooperativity, E3 abundance, time dependence, the hook effect, and combined inhibition and degradation. Its minimum mechanistic inputs are target and E3 concentrations, target and E3 binding affinities, cooperativity, intracellular degrader concentration, target half-life, simulation time, and a catalytic degradation constant. The same system can also be represented empirically from time-resolved concentration-response data using Dmax, DC50, and endogenous turnover.
Du and colleagues require target and E3 copy number, target half-life, degrader-target KD, degrader-E3 KD, cooperativity, intracellular degrader concentration, simulation time, and a degradation observation from which kpr is fitted.
The implementations have differences. Du and colleagues update equilibrium complex abundance as the target is depleted, while Haid and Reichel developed an unsaturated approximation after presenting the fuller equilibrium expression. Nevertheless, the algebra shows substantial continuity. A new name for the effective constant does not demonstrate a new mechanistic quantity.
My interpretation. The contribution is strongest as an implementation and application: integrating proteomics inputs, calibrating systems with limited degradation data, and presenting an accessible landscape. The approach still requires several difficult-to-measure or assumed inputs. Establishing that it performs better requires a comparison with the earlier framework using matched inputs and withheld observations.

title: What a degradability landscape can tell us about protein degraders
section: What does a fitted processing constant actually contain?
text:
What does a fitted processing constant actually contain?
The paper estimates \(k_{\mathrm{pr}}\) after supplying other parameters, including target half-life, protein abundance, binding affinity, and cooperativity. Some come from public datasets; others are approximated.
My concern is that degradation data constrain the combined action of processing and engagement:
\[
k_{\mathrm{induced}}=k_{\mathrm{pr}}TE.
\]
If modeled engagement is too low, a larger fitted processing constant can compensate. A unique numerical fit therefore need not identify a unique biological mechanism.
For example, in a weak-occupancy regime, ternary-complex abundance is approximately proportional to effective E3 concentration. Underestimating that concentration threefold can inflate the fitted processing constant approximately threefold while preserving the predicted degradation response. Exposure and cooperativity errors can produce similar compensation.
This does not make the parameter useless. It makes its interpretation conditional. A low fitted value might reflect inefficient ubiquitination or proteasomal processing, but it might also reflect incorrect assumptions about intracellular exposure or accessible protein pools. Those explanations imply different medicinal-chemistry decisions.

title: What a degradability landscape can tell us about protein degraders
section: A correlation of 0.95 with conditional reconstruction
text:
A correlation of 0.95 with conditional reconstruction
In the BTK analysis, the authors fixed the measured BTK KD, target and CRBN copy numbers, BTK half-life, degrader-CRBN KD, cooperativity, and a 24-hour simulation window. They then varied kpr until the model’s simulated absolute DC50 matched the experimentally measured DC50, and used that fitted kpr to calculate DMAX.
The required inputs for each compound-cell-line observation were:

Fix the experimentally measured BTK binding \(K_D\).
Fix externally supplied parameters:

BTK copy number: 22,692 molecules/cell
CRBN copy number: 12,265 molecules/cell
BTK half-life: 71.9 h
degrader–CRBN \(K_D\): 3.84 μM
cooperativity: \(\alpha=1\)
simulation time: 24 h

Measured DC50, used to select the closest fitted kpr.

Therefore, the reported r = 0.95 does not represent an independent prediction from biochemical parameters. DC50 and DMAX were generated from the same degradation assay, and DC50 was used to calibrate the model before DMAX was estimated. The analysis is best described as conditional reconstruction. The robustness and transferability of kpr therefore remain open questions.
The rationale rests on a familiar mass-balance principle: changed protein level equals intrinsic synthesis minus intrinsic degradation minus degrader-induced degradation. The authors add PLE, the modeled ternary-complex concentration, which can represent cellular engagement more explicitly. However, PLE requires several inputs, some of which are difficult to measure and others of which are estimated. Those assumptions can reduce the reliability of the inferred kpr.
There is also a consequential definition issue. This paper uses absolute DC50, the concentration producing 50% depletion. The earlier framework uses half-maximal degradation, meaning half of DMAX. For a Hill-one concentration-response curve, algebra gives:
\[
DC_{50,\mathrm{absolute}}=\frac{DC_{50,\mathrm{relative}}}{2D_{\max}-1}.
\]
At 60% DMAX, absolute DC50 is five times relative DC50. Below 50% DMAX, absolute DC50 does not exist. The THP-1 observation with 36% DMAX is consequently absent from the comparison.
This selection is understandable, but it limits the claim: the analysis does not establish that the model distinguishes effective from ineffective degraders. Nor is the DMAX prediction an exact tautology; DMAX was not directly fitted, and the relationship still imposes a constraint.
Within-cell correlations are approximately 0.918 in Ramos and 0.916 in THP-1. Those values are high, but they should not be read as proof of accurate absolute prediction. Removing the low-DMAX Ramos observation reduces the correlation to approximately 0.526 among the remaining six compounds, whose observed DMAX values span only 84-87%.
The defensible criticism is specific: a small, selected dataset shows ordering with substantial calibration error, and performance within a narrow chemical response range is sensitive to an influential observation.

title: Drug-target landscape
text:
This public, versioned resource maps the approved-drug target landscape from the paper supplements and adds normalized drug–target relationships, target-class browsing, a separately sourced clinical pilot, and an initial U.S. FDA primary-indication layer. FDA indication coverage is partial: as of October 13, 2026, 164 of 1,766 catalog drugs have a verified earliest indication; 1,602 remain pending review. Pending records are not evidence that a drug lacks FDA approval. The clinical pilot is selected rather than comprehensive, and its outcome records should be read with their linked evidence.

  
  
    Paper baseline: The evolving landscape of drug targets. This release also adds a separately sourced clinical pilot and a primary-indication layer sourced from FDA approval records and labels.
    What has been added, and what is still uncertain?
      Beyond the paper supplements, this release adds normalized target and drug identifiers, primary/secondary target roles, target-protein classification, registry-linked clinical programs and trial protocols (including one merged ClinicalTrials.gov NCT alias), outcome-review records, coverage-quality reporting, and an initial indication-level U.S. FDA layer for selected drugs. The cards above show current release counts. When a drug's primary mechanism cannot be assigned to one protein, it appears under an explicit unclear-target entry rather than a speculative protein. Clinical records are a separate, selected pilot evidence layer, not paper-derived data; their outcome evidence also draws on linked publications, sponsor disclosures, and regulatory records.
      Interpretation limits: Target classes include non-core and unresolved-scope records, so all-target counts are not the paper's approved-target count. Approval records belong to drugs, not automatically to every linked protein or indication. Clinical event labels describe cited trial or program events, not unique failed drugs or proof that a protein target failed. Nine pilot programs remain held from headline analyses pending evidence review; an unknown stopping cause remains unknown.
      Construction note: AI-assisted extraction, coding, and drafting contributed to this resource. The release passed scripted data and source-link checks, but its selected clinical pilot is not a systematic review; verify consequential interpretations against the linked primary sources.
